subject: English
chapter_title: Where Do All the Teachers Go?
learning_objectives: Read and recite the poem 'Where Do All the Teachers Go?' with correct rhythm and expression
Identify the humorous questions the child asks about teachers' lives outside school
Understand the central theme: children see teachers as special, not ordinary humans
Appreciate the poem's gentle humour and the child's curiosity and imagination
Identify poetic devices used: rhyme scheme, repetition, rhetorical questions, and humour
Understand the meaning of key vocabulary from the poem
Recognise the child's plan to write a poem about the teacher — and what this reveals
Answer comprehension and MCQ questions accurately based on the poem
prerequisite_knowledge: Basic understanding of what a poem is — stanzas, rhyme, rhythm
Understanding of rhetorical questions (questions asked for effect, not expecting a real answer)
Familiarity with the concept that teachers are authority figures in school life
Basic reading comprehension skills to understand humour in a poem

introduction.why_important: This poem explores a very relatable childhood thought: do teachers exist outside school? By making students laugh and think, it gently teaches them that teachers are full human beings with real lives — a lesson in empathy and perspective-taking.
introduction.real_life_relevance: Every student has had the strange experience of seeing their teacher outside school — at a supermarket or on a bus — and feeling genuinely surprised. This poem captures that exact feeling in a funny, warm way. It reminds students that the people who teach them are people first.
introduction.karnataka_context: In Karnataka, teachers hold a deeply honoured place in society — the Kannada saying 'Guru Devo Bhava' (the teacher is like God) reflects this. Teachers' Day on 5 September is widely celebrated in Karnataka schools with special programmes, speeches, and gifts. The poem's gentle questioning of teachers' human lives is not disrespectful — it is a child's curious, imaginative way of honouring the mystery of the person who seems to live entirely for school. Karnataka's own tradition of Guru-Shishya (teacher-student) relationships in classical music, dance, and learning makes this theme deeply resonant.
introduction.connection_to_previous_learning: This poem connects thematically to Chapter 11 (Vocation) — both poems are told from a child's perspective and both show how children imagine the lives of adults they encounter. In 'Vocation', the child imagines workers as free; here, the child imagines teachers as so special they might not be ordinary humans at all.

poem_text.stanza_1: Where do all the teachers go / When it's four o'clock? / Do they live in houses / And do they wash their socks?
poem_text.stanza_2: Do they wear pyjamas / And do they watch TV? / And do they pick their noses / The same as you and me?
poem_text.stanza_3: Do they live with other people / Have they mums and dads? / And were they ever children / And were they ever bad?
poem_text.stanza_4: Did they ever, never spell right / Did they ever make mistakes? / Were they punished in the corner / If they pinched the chocolate flakes?
poem_text.stanza_5: Did they ever lose their hymn books / Did they ever leave their greens? / Did they scribble on the desk tops / Did they wear old dirty jeans?
poem_text.stanza_6: I'll follow one back home today / I'll find out what they do / Then I'll put it in a poem / That they can read to you.

characters.name: The Child (Speaker)
characters.role: A curious school student who wonders whether teachers live normal human lives outside school — washing socks, watching TV, picking noses, having parents, making mistakes — and plans to follow one home to find out

characters.name: The Teachers (Subject)
characters.role: The unnamed teachers who are the subject of the child's curiosity. They are never shown directly — we only see how the child imagines them. Their mystery is the engine of the poem

plot: The child wonders where teachers go when school ends at four o'clock. Do they simply vanish? Do they live in houses?
The child asks a series of funny questions about teachers' everyday habits: do they wash socks, wear pyjamas, watch TV, pick their noses?
The child wonders if teachers live with other people and have parents of their own — mums and dads.
The child asks if teachers were ever children themselves — and if they were ever naughty: did they spell wrong, make mistakes, get punished?
More humorous questions: did they lose their hymn books, leave vegetables uneaten, scribble on desks, wear old dirty jeans?
In the final stanza, the child reveals a plan: to follow a teacher home, find out what they really do, and write a poem about it that the teacher can read aloud to students.
story_summary.moral: Teachers are ordinary human beings with real lives, feelings, and even past mistakes — just like their students. Children should see their teachers as people, not just authority figures. The poem also celebrates the child's creative instinct: turning curiosity into a poem is an act of imagination and empathy.

core_concepts.simple_explanation: Children often think teachers are so special that they must be different from ordinary people. This poem shows that funny, curious side of how students see their teachers.
core_concepts.detailed_explanation: At the heart of this poem is a child's inability to imagine a teacher as an ordinary person. To young students, teachers seem to exist only inside school — always formal, always in charge, always knowing the answers. The idea that a teacher might watch television in pyjamas, pick their nose, or wear dirty jeans seems almost impossible. This is because children place teachers on a pedestal — they are authority figures who represent knowledge, rules, and correction. The poem gently dismantles this image by asking increasingly human, even silly questions. Each question reveals one more layer of ordinary humanity that the child struggles to attribute to the teacher. By the final stanza, the child has a plan — to follow the teacher and write about what they find. This shows that the child's curiosity is not disrespectful but imaginative, and that the poem itself is an act of trying to understand an adult who seems mysterious.
core_concepts.real_life_example: Imagine seeing your maths teacher at a vegetable market carrying a bag of onions, wearing a casual shirt. Most students feel a strange shock — 'Sir/Ma'am eats onions?! Sir/Ma'am goes shopping?!' This is the exact feeling the poem explores. Teachers seem to belong only to school, so seeing them in a normal setting feels almost unreal.
core_concepts.karnataka_example: In Karnataka, the tradition of Guru Purnima and Teachers' Day celebrations involves students treating teachers with almost sacred respect — garlanding them, touching their feet, writing poems and speeches about them. This elevation of teachers in Karnataka's culture makes the poem especially resonant: the child's belief that teachers are extraordinary is not unusual in the Indian context. The poem gently humanises this elevated image.
core_concepts.common_mistakes: Students sometimes think the poem is making fun of teachers or being disrespectful. It is not. The poem's tone is warm, curious, and affectionate — not mocking. The child asks funny questions because they genuinely cannot imagine the teacher as human, not because they want to insult them. The humour comes from the gap between the teacher's school image and ordinary human reality.
core_concepts.memory_tip: Think of it as the TEACHER MYSTERY: T-E-A-C-H-E-R = Totally Extraordinary Adults Children Have Enormous Respect for. The poem is about gently solving that mystery!

core_concepts.concept_name: Rhetorical Questions as a Poetic Device
core_concepts.simple_explanation: A rhetorical question is a question asked for effect — not because you expect a real answer. The poem is full of them: 'Do they wash their socks?' is not a real question requiring an answer; it is a way of expressing wonder.
core_concepts.detailed_explanation: Almost the entire poem (stanzas 1 through 5) consists of rhetorical questions. Peter Dixon uses questions as the primary poetic device — not statements, not descriptions, but a series of curious, escalating questions. This structure is clever for two reasons. First, it puts the reader in the child's position: we experience the curiosity directly, rather than being told about it. Second, it creates a building rhythm — each question leading to the next, like a child who cannot stop wondering. The questions also serve a humorous purpose: they escalate from the relatively normal ('Do they live in houses?') to the very funny ('Do they pick their noses?'). This escalation mirrors how a curious child's mind works — starting with reasonable questions and spiralling into increasingly comic territory.
core_concepts.real_life_example: When a student says 'Are you serious right now?!' or 'Is this actually happening?!' in a surprised moment, they are using rhetorical questions — not expecting a literal yes/no answer, but expressing strong emotion. The poet uses the same technique across the entire poem to express the child's growing wonder.
core_concepts.karnataka_example: In the Vachana poetry tradition of Karnataka — particularly in the works of saints like Akka Mahadevi and Basavanna — rhetorical questions were a key device. Basavanna's vachanas often asked 'How can I know the Lord?' or 'What is true worship?' — not expecting direct answers, but prompting spiritual reflection. Peter Dixon's rhetorical questions serve a similar function: not to get answers, but to make the reader think and feel.
core_concepts.common_mistakes: Students often try to answer the rhetorical questions in the poem as if they were real questions. For example, 'Do they wash their socks? — Yes, teachers wash their socks.' While this is technically correct, it misses the point. The questions are not really asking for information — they are expressing the child's amazed, humorous curiosity. The value of the question is in its asking, not its answering.
core_concepts.memory_tip: RHETORICAL = Really Having Effect Through Obvious Reasons — It's Called Asking for Laughs! In this poem, every '?' is really a '!' in disguise — it expresses emotion, not a request for information.

core_concepts.simple_explanation: The poem is funny — questions like 'do they pick their noses?' make us laugh. But behind the humour is a deeper lesson: learning to see others as full human beings, not just roles.
core_concepts.detailed_explanation: Peter Dixon uses humour as a vehicle for empathy. On the surface, the poem is funny — the image of a strict teacher in pyjamas watching TV or picking their nose is comically incongruous. But beneath the laughter, the poem is teaching something profound: everyone — including people in authority — is a full human being with ordinary habits, past mistakes, and a private life. The child's questions, though funny, are actually acts of empathy in the making. By imagining the teacher as someone who was once a child, who once made spelling mistakes and got punished, the child begins to close the gap between 'student' and 'teacher'. The final stanza is particularly powerful: the child plans to write a poem and share it with the teacher — turning curiosity into creativity and connection. Humour here is not a barrier to understanding but a bridge to it.
core_concepts.real_life_example: When students laugh together about a teacher's habit — the way they always say 'Okay class, quiet please' or tap the board when thinking — they are actually practising a gentle form of humanising. The laughter is not mean; it shows awareness of the teacher as a person with quirks, not just a function. This poem teaches students to move from laughing at to understanding.
core_concepts.karnataka_example: Karnataka's Yakshagana and folk theatre traditions use humour (especially through the 'Hasyagaras' — comic characters) to make serious observations about human nature accessible to all audiences. Similarly, Peter Dixon uses the child's funny questions to make the serious point that authority figures are human beings accessible to a Grade 6 student. Humour as a vehicle for truth is a time-honoured tradition in Karnataka's arts.
core_concepts.common_mistakes: Students sometimes feel the poem is too silly to have a serious message. This is incorrect — humour and depth are not opposites. Some of the most profound messages in literature are delivered through comedy. The child's plan in the last stanza to 'put it in a poem that they can read to you' is genuinely moving — it shows the child's desire to connect with the teacher, not mock them.
core_concepts.memory_tip: HE = Humour + Empathy. Every funny question in the poem is also an empathy question in disguise: 'Were they ever children?' = 'Are they like me?' LAUGH first, UNDERSTAND after — that is how this poem works!

key_terms_glossary.meaning: A question asked for effect or to express a point, not to get a real answer. Almost every question in this poem is rhetorical — the child is not literally expecting the teacher to answer whether they wash their socks; the questions express wonder and curiosity.

Loose, comfortable clothing worn for sleeping. The child asks if teachers wear pyjamas — imagining the teacher in such casual, domestic clothing is funny because teachers are always seen in formal, authoritative attire in school.

A book of religious songs (hymns) used in school assemblies or church services. In the poem, the child asks if teachers ever lost their hymn books — something students themselves frequently do — implying teachers might have been just as forgetful as students.

Stole or took secretly, especially food. 'Were they punished in the corner / If they pinched the chocolate flakes?' — the child imagines that teachers, when they were children, might have secretly stolen a snack and been punished for it, just like students today.
Green vegetables such as spinach, beans, or peas. 'Did they ever leave their greens?' means did teachers, as children, refuse to eat their vegetables — a very common childhood behaviour.
key_terms_glossary.story_context: The child imagines the teacher as a child who disliked eating vegetables, just as students themselves do.

key_terms_glossary.meaning: To write or draw carelessly or messily. 'Did they scribble on the desk tops?' — the child wonders if teachers once wrote or drew on desks, something that is normally forbidden and for which students get scolded.
The pattern of rhymes at the end of lines in a poem. In this poem, alternate lines rhyme (ABCB pattern — the second and fourth lines of each stanza rhyme), giving the poem a song-like, bouncy rhythm.

The quality of being funny or amusing. Peter Dixon uses humour throughout the poem — asking funny questions about teachers' private habits — to make a gentle, deeper point about seeing teachers as human beings.
A group of lines forming a unit in a poem, like a paragraph in prose. 'Where Do All the Teachers Go?' has six stanzas, each with four lines.

The ability to understand and share the feelings of another person. The final stanza of the poem shows the child developing empathy — trying to understand the teacher's life not to mock but to write about it and share it with others.

worked_examples.question: What are the 'normal' things the child imagines teachers might do? List at least five from the poem.
step_by_step_answer: Step 1: Read through the poem stanza by stanza, noting every human activity the child wonders about.
Step 2: Stanza 1 — live in houses, wash their socks.
Step 3: Stanza 2 — wear pyjamas, watch TV, pick their noses.
Step 4: Stanza 3 — live with other people, have mums and dads, were once children, were once bad.
Step 5: Stanza 4 — made spelling mistakes, were punished in the corner, pinched chocolate flakes.
Step 6: Stanza 5 — lost hymn books, left greens uneaten, scribbled on desk tops, wore old dirty jeans.

Conclusion: The child imagines teachers doing at least twelve normal, everyday human activities. By listing so many, the poem shows how thoroughly the child has separated the teacher's school image from a possible ordinary human life.

worked_examples.question: Use the word 'scribble' in a sentence connected to the poem 'Where Do All the Teachers Go?'
step_by_step_answer: Step 1: Recall meaning — 'Scribble' means to write or draw carelessly and messily.
Step 2: Connect to poem — The child asks 'Did they scribble on the desk tops?' — wondering if teachers, as children, did the same naughty things that students do today.

Step 3: Write sentence: 'The child in the poem wondered whether teachers, when they were young, used to scribble on their desk tops just like students sometimes do today — and whether they too were scolded for it.'

worked_examples.question: The poem suggests that teachers were once children who made mistakes. How does understanding this change the way you think about your own teachers?
step_by_step_answer: Step 1: State what the poem suggests — The child asks 'Were they ever children and were they ever bad? Did they ever, never spell right? Did they ever make mistakes?' This implies that teachers were once students themselves — imperfect, sometimes naughty, and learning.
Step 2: Think about your own experience — When you make a mistake in class and feel embarrassed, it can seem like the teacher has never made such a mistake. This poem asks you to reconsider.

Step 3: Apply the lesson — Knowing that teachers were once students who also struggled, made spelling mistakes, and got punished can make the teacher-student relationship feel less intimidating and more human.

Step 4: Connect to empathy — When you see your teacher not just as someone who corrects you but as someone who was once corrected themselves, you begin to practise empathy — understanding another person's experience.

Conclusion: The poem teaches that seeing teachers as full human beings — with a childhood, mistakes, and an ordinary home life — helps students relate to them better, reducing fear and building genuine respect.

questions.q: Who wrote the poem 'Where Do All the Teachers Go?'?
questions.a: The poem was written by Peter Dixon, a British poet known for humorous and child-friendly verse.

questions.q: At what time does the child wonder where teachers go?
questions.a: The child wonders where teachers go at four o'clock — when school ends. The poem opens with 'Where do all the teachers go / When it's four o'clock?'

questions.q: Why does the child find it hard to imagine teachers living in houses and washing socks?
questions.a: The child sees teachers only in the context of school — as authority figures who are always formal, knowledgeable, and in control. Imagining them doing ordinary domestic things like washing socks seems strange because the child has placed teachers on a pedestal above everyday human life.

questions.q: What does the child's plan in the last stanza tell us about the child's character?
questions.a: The child plans to follow a teacher home, find out what they do, and write a poem about it. This shows the child is curious, imaginative, and creative. It also shows the child wants to understand teachers better — which is an act of empathy. The plan to write a poem shows the child's literary instinct.

questions.q: If you were to write a similar poem about a person in your life, who would you choose and what questions would you ask?
questions.a: Answers will vary. A student might choose a parent, a shopkeeper, or a school principal. The key is that the questions should reveal what the child cannot imagine that person doing outside their known role.

key_takeaways: The poem 'Where Do All the Teachers Go?' is written by Peter Dixon, a British poet.
The speaker is a school student who wonders whether teachers live normal human lives after school ends at four o'clock.
The child asks funny, escalating questions: do teachers wash socks, wear pyjamas, watch TV, pick noses, have parents, make mistakes?
The poem has six stanzas with four lines each, following an ABCB rhyme scheme (second and fourth lines rhyme).
The poem's central theme is children's perception of teachers as special or superhuman — and the gentle truth that teachers are ordinary human beings.
Key poetic devices: rhetorical questions (all the 'Do they...?' questions), rhyme scheme (ABCB), humour, and repetition.
The final stanza reveals the child's plan: to follow a teacher home, find out the truth, and write a poem about it.
The deeper message: developing empathy by imagining others' full humanity — teachers were once children who also made mistakes.
Karnataka connection: the poem resonates with Karnataka's tradition of honouring teachers (Guru Purnima, Teachers' Day) — it gently humanises the revered teacher figure.
Tone of the poem: warm, humorous, curious, and affectionate — not mocking or disrespectful.

revision_notes: The poem 'Where Do All the Teachers Go?' is written by Peter Dixon, a British poet. It is a humorous, six-stanza poem with four lines per stanza, following an ABCB rhyme scheme (second and fourth lines of each stanza rhyme). The speaker is a school-going child who wonders where teachers go when school ends at four o'clock. The child asks a series of funny rhetorical questions about teachers' private lives: Do they live in houses? Wash their socks? Wear pyjamas? Watch TV? Pick their noses? Have mums and dads? Were they ever children? Were they ever bad? Did they make spelling mistakes, get punished, scribble on desks, lose hymn books, leave vegetables uneaten, or wear dirty jeans? The questions escalate from the everyday to the amusingly naughty, showing how thoroughly the child has separated the teacher from ordinary humanity. In the final stanza, the child reveals a plan: to follow a teacher home, discover the truth, and write a poem about it to share with the class. The poem's central theme is children's tendency to see teachers as extraordinary beings rather than ordinary people. Its deeper message is about empathy — the child is trying to imagine the teacher's full human life. Key poetic devices: rhetorical questions, ABCB rhyme scheme, humour, and repetition ('Did they ever...'). Key vocabulary: rhetorical question, pyjamas, hymn book, pinched, greens, scribble, stanza. The tone is warm, funny, and affectionate — never mocking.

The poem has six stanzas with four lines each.
Rhyme scheme: ABCB — the second and fourth lines of each stanza rhyme.
The child asks where teachers go at four o'clock — when school ends.
Funny questions: do they wash socks, wear pyjamas, watch TV, pick their noses, have mums and dads?
The child wonders if teachers were ever children who made mistakes, got punished, scribbled on desks.
Final stanza: the child plans to follow a teacher home, find out the truth, and write a poem about it.
Central theme: children see teachers as extraordinary; the poem gently reveals that teachers are ordinary humans.
Key poetic devices: rhetorical questions, ABCB rhyme scheme, humour, repetition.
The poem's tone is warm and affectionate — it humanises teachers with gentle, funny curiosity, not mockery.
